summary: Provides a mechanism by which FTP clients can discover which new features a given FTP server supports, through a FEAT command and an option negotiation.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2389 gives the File Transfer Protocol a way to ask what a server can do. The client sends FEAT, and the server answers with a list of the extensions it supports, one per line. The client can then use OPTS to choose how a later command should behave, such as which format to list files in. The two commands are additions, so older servers simply answer that they do not know them.

questions: how to list ftp server features
what is the ftp feat command
what is the ftp opts command
subtitle: Two FTP commands, FEAT and OPTS, let a client discover what a server supports and choose options.

tldr.problem: FTP keeps gaining new commands and options, and no client can assume a particular server implements any of them. Without a way to ask, a client has to try each extension in turn, which is wasteful and may trigger side effects.
tldr.mechanism: The FEAT command asks the server to list the extensions it supports, one per line, in a 211 multiline reply. The OPTS command then sets the options for a later FTP command, and is required wherever FEAT is implemented.
tldr.outcome: A client learns the server's capabilities in one exchange and can assume that the only extensions the server has are the ones listed. The memo also warns that an error reply does not prove an older extension is missing, because several were widely used before FEAT existed.

facts.label: Feature listing reply
facts.value: 211- then one feature line each, ending with 211 End

today: RFC 2389 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It amends RFC 959 by adding two commands and leaves every existing command untouched, and it was developed in the FTPEXT Working Group of the IETF.

sections.title: Why FTP Needed a Way to Ask
sections.content:
RFC 2389 amends the File Transfer Protocol, RFC 959, by adding two commands, FEAT and OPTS. Together they let a client discover which optional commands a server supports and how they are supported, and let the client select among the options that any FTP command may offer.

The problem is that FTP is extended from time to time, and implementations cannot be assumed to implement newly defined mechanisms straight away. Without a standard way to ask, a client has to try each extension in turn, which costs a series of exchanges between the user and server processes. The memo notes that this may not always even be possible, because issuing a command merely to find out whether it is supported can have an effect that is not wanted.

The memo also points out that a server which supports FEAT must list every properly documented FTP extension it has, including ones that existed long before FEAT was adopted. So when a client receives a FEAT reply, it can assume the only extensions the server supports are the ones listed. The converse does not hold: an error reply to FEAT does not mean older extensions are missing, because several were developed and widely used before this document existed, and a client that cares should test for those individually.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP gains new commands over the years, and servers pick them up at different times. Without a way to ask, a client has to try each one in turn, and a command sent just to test it can have side effects. FEAT turns that into a single question with a single answer.

sections.title: Conventions and Tokens
sections.content:
The memo uses the document conventions of BCP 14, RFC 2119, so words such as MUST and SHOULD carry their usual requirement levels. Terms defined in RFC 959 are used as defined there, including ASCII, reply, server-FTP process, user-FTP process, server-PI, user-PI and user.

Syntax is written in the Augmented BNF of RFC 2234, with the basic elements such as ALPHA, DIGIT, VCHAR and SP taken from Appendix A of that document. One new token is added, TCHAR, which is a visible character or a space or a horizontal tab.

Two reply rules are set out. An error response is an error code, a space, any number of TCHARs and a line ending, where the error code is the digit 4 or 5 followed by two digits. The reply conventions of Section 4.2 of RFC 959 are used unchanged, but the memo warns implementors that the ABNF in FTP documents often shows replies in the one line form, and that this does not mean a multiline reply is not permitted: unless stated otherwise, any reply to any FTP command, including QUIT, may be multiline. Replies are identified throughout by their three digit code, so the 500 Reply means the reply whose code is 500.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo borrows the requirement words and the syntax notation used elsewhere, and it adds one new character type for replies. It also repeats a warning: a reply shown on one line in a syntax rule may still be sent as several lines.

sections.title: The FEAT Command and Its Reply
sections.content:
The FEAT command consists of nothing but the word FEAT. It has no parameters and no arguments, and giving it any is a syntax error, which the server answers with 501. A server that does not support FEAT at all answers 500 or 502, which is the normal reply to any unknown command. A server that recognizes FEAT but implements no extended features, and so has nothing to report, should answer with the no-features reply 211, though it may use 500 or 502 instead, because the two cases are practically indistinguishable. The no-features reply must not use the multiline format: exactly one response line is required and permitted.

A full reply is a multiline one. The first line is 211- followed by free-form text that is not interpreted and has no practical use, since it is not expected to be shown to end users. Then come one or more feature lines, each beginning with a single space, and the reply ends with the line 211 End. The space at the start of a feature line is not optional and is not general white space: it guarantees that a feature line can never be mistaken for the end of the listing, and it is required even where there is no possibility of ambiguity.

A feature line is a feature label, optionally followed by a space and the parameters of that feature. Each extension must be listed on its own line, so that the listing can carry the parameters each extension supports. The label to use is fixed by the document that defines the extension. It is often the name of a new command, but that is not required, and a feature need not add a command at all. Any parameters are specified together with the command they belong to, and that specification also says how the parameters are to be interpreted. The labels and parameters are nominally case sensitive, but the definitions usually make them case independent, and implementations are recommended to use upper case when transmitting the reply.

FEAT itself is not listed among the features, and support for FEAT is shown by the server giving a reply other than 500 or 502. Clients must expect to see features they do not recognise in the reply. That is not an error; it means the server has implemented a specification the client has not heard of. The order of the features carries no meaning, and a server need not return the same order twice.
sections.plainLanguage: FEAT takes no arguments. The server answers with a 211 reply that lists one extension per line, each line starting with a space, and closes the list with the line 211 End. A server with no extensions to report answers with a single 211 line. A client should expect to see names it does not recognise, and the order of the list carries no meaning.

sections.title: Why FEAT Is Worth Having
sections.content:
The memo argues that a standard way for the server to tell the client which features and extensions it supports is not absolutely necessary, but it will cut down on unnecessary traffic between the two as more extensions are introduced. Without such a mechanism the user process would have to try each extension in turn, producing a series of exchanges. Besides being wasteful, that procedure may not always be possible, because a command issued only to find out whether it is supported can have an effect that is not desired.

The FEAT reply is therefore the negotiated starting point: the client learns everything the server has in one exchange, and can then decide which of the optional commands it will actually use.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says FEAT is not strictly necessary, but it saves traffic and avoids commands that were sent only to test something. One exchange replaces a whole series of trial commands.

sections.title: The OPTS Command
sections.content:
The OPTS command lets a user process specify how the server should behave when another FTP command, the target command, is issued later. The exact behaviour and syntax vary with the target command and are specified in the definition of that command. Where no behaviour is defined for a command, there are no options available for it.

The request syntax is the word opts, a space, the name of a command that allows options, and optionally a space and the options themselves, in the format that command specifies. The response is either a 200 reply, which is the good case, or a bad case that is either 451 or 501.

A 200 reply must be sent when the command name is recognised and the command options, if any, are recognised and appropriate. Otherwise a bad reply is sent. A 501 reply is right for any permanent error, meaning any case where simply repeating the command later, with no other change of state, would also be an error. A 451 reply is right where some temporary condition at the server, not related to the state of the conversation between user and server, stops the command being accepted, but where a changed environment later might let it succeed. If the server does not recognise OPTS at all, it answers 500 or 502 in the usual way.

OPTS must be implemented wherever FEAT is implemented, so there is no entry in the FEAT list for OPTS itself. Neither command has any optional functionality, so there are no OPTS FEAT and OPTS OPTS commands.
sections.plainLanguage: OPTS sets how the server should behave the next time a particular command is used, for example which format a listing should take. A 200 reply means the setting was accepted, 451 means the server was busy at that moment, and 501 means the setting was wrong and will stay wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo believes no significant new security issues, beyond those already present in FTP, are created by this extension. It does note one consequence: FEAT gives users a way to find out the capabilities of a server, and extra information may be deduced from the answer. The same basic information could be obtained by probing the server for the various commands, but without FEAT that probing would show up in the server's logs as attempts to reach extension commands, which might reveal an attacker. The memo does not consider this a serious enough threat to warrant any remedial action.

The security of any additional features reported by FEAT and manipulated by OPTS should be addressed in the documents that define those features.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo finds no new security problem, with one small note. FEAT lets a client read off a server's capabilities in one go, which is information an attacker might also want. The memo does not think that is worth acting on.

viz.caption: A TYPICAL FEAT REPLY, VERBATIM FROM RFC 2389

data.title: FEAT and its reply
data.code:
C> feat
S> 211-Extensions supported:
S>  MLST size*;create;modify*;perm;media-type
S>  SIZE
S>  COMPRESSION
S>  MDTM
S> 211 END

viz.caption: WHAT A FEAT REPLY TELLS THE CLIENT

items.title: One question
items.text: FEAT takes no arguments, so there is nothing to get wrong when asking.

items.title: Unknown names are normal
items.text: A client must expect to see features it does not recognise. That is not an error.

items.title: A complete list
items.text: The reply names every documented extension the server has, including ones older than FEAT.

items.title: Order means nothing
items.text: The server may return the features in a different order each time.

items.title: No OPTS entry
items.text: OPTS is not listed, because a server that supports FEAT must support OPTS.

viz.caption: REPLY CODES USED BY FEAT AND OPTS

items.label: No features
items.desc: The server recognises FEAT but has no extended features to report. Exactly one line, never multiline.

items.label: Feature listing
items.desc: The first line of a multiline listing, followed by one feature per line and a closing 211 End line.

items.label: Option accepted
items.desc: The OPTS command name and its options were recognised and appropriate.

items.label: Temporary failure
items.desc: A temporary condition at the server stopped the command being accepted; it may succeed later.

items.label: Command not recognised
items.desc: The normal reply to a command the server does not know, including FEAT and OPTS.

items.label: Syntax error
items.desc: Errors in the command syntax, such as giving parameters to FEAT. Also any permanent error from OPTS.

items.label: Command not implemented
items.desc: The server recognises the command name but does not implement it, including FEAT and OPTS.

data.title: OPTS request and response syntax
data.code:
opts             = opts-cmd SP command-name
                   [ SP command-options ] CRLF
opts-cmd         = "opts"
command-name     = <any FTP command which allows option setting>
command-options  = <format specified by individual FTP command>

opts-response    = opts-good / opts-bad
opts-good        = "200" SP response-message CRLF
opts-bad         = "451" SP response-message CRLF /
                   "501" SP response-message CRLF
response-message = *TCHAR
